lessons.title: Variables & Data Types

sections.content: Variables are named containers used to store data values. In modern JavaScript, we declare variables using 'const' for constant values that won't be reassigned, and 'let' for variables whose values may change over time.

sections.title: Best Practice
sections.content: Always default to using 'const'. Only use 'let' when you know the variable's value needs to change later in execution. Avoid using 'var' in modern code!

JavaScript supports several core data types:
• Strings: Text enclosed in quotes or backticks
• Numbers: Integers and decimals
• Booleans: true or false
• Arrays: Ordered lists of items
• Objects: Key-value data collections
• typeof: Operator to check a variable's data type

objectives: Declare variables using const and let keywords correctly
Work with primitive data types: strings, numbers, and booleans
Store multi-value collections using arrays and objects
Inspect data types using the typeof operator
lessons.mentorTip: Use template literals (`Hello ${name}`) when building strings with variables — it's cleaner than string concatenation with +.

lessons.title: Functions & Scope

sections.content: Functions are reusable blocks of code designed to perform specific tasks. They take inputs (parameters), execute logic, and can return an output value using the 'return' statement.

sections.title: Pro Tip
sections.content: Keep functions small and focused on a single task. This makes your code easier to test, read, and maintain.

Scope defines where variables are accessible in your code:
• Global Scope: Declared outside any function, accessible everywhere.
• Local/Function Scope: Declared inside a function, accessible only within that function.
• Block Scope: Declared with let/const inside { }, accessible only inside that block.

objectives: Write reusable functions with parameters and return values
Distinguish between function parameters and arguments
Understand global, function/local, and block variable scopes
lessons.mentorTip: Always specify return values when a function needs to compute and pass data back to the caller.
